name: Yerba Buena Center for the Arts

facts.text: Opened on October 12, 1993.
The Galleries and Forum building was designed by Fumihiko Maki; the theater by the Polshek Partnership.
A theater company founded in 1993 by David Dower, growing out of the Z Collective.
Moved into this full-time Mission District facility in 2009.
A bronze statue about 10 feet tall of three girls from China, Korea and the Philippines holding hands.
A bronze figure of an elderly woman stands beside the pedestal looking up at the girls.
Stands in St. Mary's Square.
A bronze statue in Civic Center owned by the San Francisco Arts Commission.
Replaced a plaster Lincoln statue erected in 1866 and destroyed in the fire after the 1906 earthquake.
Sculpted by Douglas Tilden and commissioned by Mayor James D. Phelan, who paid the $12,000 cost.
Commemorates California Admission Day, September 9, 1850.
A marble column about 35 feet tall topped by the Genius of California, with a miner figure below.
Converted to twin theaters in 1976.
Designated San Francisco landmark number 217 on February 21, 1996.
Stopped operating as a movie theater on February 22, 1998.
A flat-bottomed scow schooner built by Fred Siemer at his boatyard at Hunters Point.
About 59 feet long, built to haul goods around San Francisco Bay.
Built with Works Progress Administration help alongside the Casting Pond.
Home of the Golden Gate Angling & Casting Club, formed in 1933.
Hosts free fly casting lessons on the second Saturday of each month.
Commissioned by the Assyrian Foundation for the Arts and presented to the city on May 29, 1988.
Shows the Assyrian king holding a clay tablet and a lion cub.

name: Bank of Canton (former Chinese Telephone Exchange)

facts.text: Housed the Chinese Telephone Exchange, which served Chinatown until dial phones arrived in the 1940s.
Women became chief operators of the Chinese Telephone Exchange in 1906.
Completed in 1901 with two 3-inch rapid-fire guns to protect the inner harbor.
Named for Lieutenant Henry Baldwin, Fifth Artillery, who died of wounds at Cedar Creek in 1864.
Completed in 1900 with four 3-inch rapid-fire guns to protect the inner harbor.
Named for Lieutenant Daniel Blaney, Third Artillery, killed at Fort Oswego, New York, in 1814.
A concrete 12-inch coastal gun battery at Fort Miley with three emplacements, completed in 1903.
Named for Major James Chester, 3rd U.S. Artillery, a Civil War veteran.
Its armament was scrapped in 1943.
Built in 1936 at Fort Funston with two 16-inch guns, each able to fire 2,100 pound shells nearly 26 miles.
Built as a buried fortification with up to 20 feet of concrete and earth cover over the guns.
One of two experimental dynamite gun batteries in the U.S.; the other was at Sandy Hook, New Jersey.
Had three 15-inch pneumatic guns that fired dynamite charges with compressed air; test-fired in December 1895.
The guns were declared obsolete and scrapped by 1901.
Completed in 1895 as Battery Howe, with four pits each armed with four 12-inch mortars.
Split in 1902 into Battery Howe (east pits) and Battery Arthur Wagner (west pits).
Cross-shaped 'Abbott Cross' design gave a 360-degree field of fire; mortars were dismounted in 1920.
An Endicott-era battery built in 1898 with three 12-inch guns on disappearing carriages.
Named for Lieutenant Colonel James Lancaster, Third Artillery, a Civil War veteran who died in 1900.
Part of a Fort Miley mortar battery completed in 1902 with sixteen 12-inch mortars in four pits.
Split in 1906 into Batteries Livingston and Springer; pits A and B kept the Livingston name.
Named for Colonel LaRhett Livingston, 3rd U.S. Artillery, who died in 1903.
Completed in 1898 as Battery Stotsenburg with four pits of four 12-inch mortars each.
Split in 1906; the western pits were renamed Battery William McKinnon.
Salvaged by order of the War Department in 1943.
Completed in 1895 with two 12-inch guns on barbette carriages.
Could fire its guns both seaward and into the bay.
Named for Captain Marion M. Saffold, 13th Infantry, killed in action at Cavite in 1899.
Completed in 1900 with two rapid-fire 5-inch guns on pedestal mounts to protect the inner harbor.
Its guns were moved to Battery Bruff at Fort Funston in 1917.
Named for Lieutenant Walter Sherwood, Seventh Infantry, killed in 1840 fighting the Seminole in Florida.
Completed in 1900 with three 8-inch guns on disappearing carriages.
Its three guns were dismounted in 1917 and sent to Watervliet Arsenal in New York.
Named for Lieutenant William A. Slaughter, Fourth Infantry, killed in Washington Territory in 1855.

name: Battery Springer A
note: Input name 'Springer A' is a pit of Battery Springer (Fort Miley); fortwiki page Battery Springer used.

facts.text: Built in 1899 as mortar pits C and D of Battery Livingston and renamed Battery Springer in 1906.
Had eight 12-inch mortars; named for Captain Anton Springer, killed in the Philippines in 1901.
Completed in 1873 as West Battery, armed with twelve 15-inch Rodman cannon.
Built on the bluffs behind Fort Point as a response to rifled guns; mostly destroyed by 1890s batteries.
Installed in 1879 as a temperance fountain donated by Henry D. Cogswell, originally at Kearny and Market Streets.
Moved to Washington Square in 1904.
A time capsule in its base was opened in 1979; a new one is due to be opened in 2079.
